clue.text: Old magazines that display the things that might make your spine lose all sensation?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: past issues of a periodical, no longer current

definitions.text: the things that might make your spine lose all sensation

explanation.walkthrough: The second half is a joke reading: something that numbs is a 'numb-er', and your spine is your back.
explanation.definitionFit: Earlier issues of a magazine or journal are known as back numbers or back issues.

clue.text: Possibly Cane's about to lavish attentions on funny stories.

indicators.note: the reworked letters go round the doting word
possibly suggests another form of the letters of Cane's

parts.note: taken as written, apostrophe dropped
to dote on someone is to lavish affection on them

explanation.surface: Someone named Cane is about to fuss over a collection of amusing tales.
explanation.definitionFit: Anecdotes are short entertaining accounts of real incidents.

clue.text: Finders, as they say, but they may be in charge.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the word that follows finders in the saying 'finders ...'
second meaning: those in charge, such as custodians or wardens

explanation.walkthrough: The playground rule 'finders keepers' gives the first sense; the second is a custodian.
explanation.definitionFit: A keeper is a guardian or custodian, someone responsible for something.

clue.text: One became a beautiful swimmer, though one of those made way for in a book is not the handsome type.

parts.note: plain-looking, the opposite of handsome

parts.words: one of those made way for in a book
parts.note: the picture book 'Make Way for Ducklings' is Robert McCloskey's classic

explanation.surface: A fairy-tale bird grew into a lovely swimmer, though as a chick it was plain.
explanation.walkthrough: In Andersen's tale the mocked chick grows into a swan, the beautiful swimmer.
explanation.definitionFit: Hans Christian Andersen's ugly duckling turns out to be a cygnet that grows into a swan.

clue.text: A real cad? No wonder such is jumpy! ("Peep" doesn't get over here.)

parts.note: the nursery rhyme shepherdess is Little Bo Peep
if you do not get over something, you go under it

explanation.surface: A scoundrel is jumpy, and Bo Peep is kept out of the picture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No wonder such is jumpy' is a joke on the word: a bounder bounds.
explanation.definitionFit: Bounder is an old-fashioned word for a dishonourable man, a cad.

clue.text: Put in a few more chips!

definitions.text: Put in a few more chips!

parts.note: read as adding to a pot, as a poker player does before others must match it
gambling tokens rather than potato or wood chips

explanation.walkthrough: In poker the ante is the stake; increasing it means putting in more chips, and figuratively raising demands.
explanation.definitionFit: To raise the ante is to increase the stake in a game, or the demands in a dispute.

clue.text: What the pitcher would hope to get without reservation.

definitions.text: What the pitcher would hope to get
definitions.meaning: first meaning: in baseball a pitcher wants every batter put out
second meaning: total, holding nothing back

explanation.walkthrough: A baseball pitcher's goal is retiring all the batters; the phrase also means wholehearted.
explanation.definitionFit: All-out describes an effort made with full commitment and nothing held back.

clue.text: The plane your uncle ended up with is a real floater.

indicators.note: the uncle word comes at the end, after the plane word

parts.note: a jet is an aircraft
Uncle Sam personifies the US

explanation.surface: A plane and Uncle Sam together turn out to be bobbing in the water.
explanation.definitionFit: Jetsam is cargo thrown overboard that may float or wash ashore.

clue.text: Sounds like an unhappy but old-fashioned miss could be found in the garden.

definitions.text: could be found in the garden
definitions.note: a descriptive phrase rather than a noun: the answer is something you could find growing in a garden

parts.note: someone blue is sad, so unhappy gives this colour word

indicators.note: the clue says the spoken phrase gives the answer, and here the miss word is heard rather than spelt

parts.note: a belle is a dated word for a beautiful young woman

explanation.surface: A forlorn, old-world young lady drifts sadly among the flower beds.
explanation.walkthrough: Blue plus belle, said aloud, is the flower's name; the definition describes where the thing is found rather than naming it.
explanation.definitionFit: The bluebell is a common woodland and garden plant with drooping blue flowers.

clue.text: The way we are supposed to stand makes an assertion that we all probably live here.

definitions.note: a clause rather than a noun: the setter, writing for an American magazine, assumes the readers' home country

parts.words: The way we are supposed to stand
parts.note: from the motto 'United we stand, divided we fall'
to state is to assert, so one who makes an assertion states

explanation.surface: A patriotic motto is quoted, and the speaker claims it describes everyone's homeland.
explanation.walkthrough: The Nation is an American weekly, so 'we all probably live here' points at its readers' country.
explanation.definitionFit: The country most readers of this American magazine live in is the USA.

clue.text: A number (a large number) pushes a pencil rather idly.

parts.note: D is the Roman numeral for five hundred
oodles is informal for a great many

explanation.surface: Someone with plenty of numbers to deal with sits scribbling absently instead.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracketed 'a large number' looks like an aside on the first number, but it supplies the rest of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: To doodle is to scribble aimlessly while your mind is elsewhere.

clue.text: The rhymes we once saw at the side of the road, or the opposite?

definitions.note: an adjective, contrary or opposing, defined here by a noun phrase

parts.words: we once saw at the side of the road
parts.note: roadside billboards are advertisements, ads for short
verse is rhyming writing

explanation.surface: A nostalgic look back at the rhyming roadside signs of old, or perhaps their reverse.
explanation.walkthrough: The picture is the Burma-Shave signs, short rhymes spread along American highways in the mid-twentieth century: advertising in verse.
explanation.definitionFit: Adverse means acting against or contrary to, as with adverse winds.

clue.text: Here you get rings around the heavenly type, with little Harold so well brought up.

parts.note: Hal is a short form of Harold

indicators.note: in a down clue, bringing a word up writes it from bottom to top

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A well-raised boy named Harold among angels and their rings.
explanation.definitionFit: Halos are the rings of light pictured above the heads of angels and saints.

clue.text: See 10
What the guy in the dell practiced.

definitions.text: What the guy in the dell practiced

parts.words: What the guy in the dell
parts.note: the nursery song 'The Farmer in the Dell' names its man only as a farmer
read as the craft or science that farmer worked at, the study of crops and soil

explanation.walkthrough: The 'guy' is the farmer of the children's song, so his practice is the science of farming.
explanation.definitionFit: Agronomy is the science of soil management and crop production, the farmer's discipline.

clue.text: In Tennessee, a point has wrongly a half-dozen on the rising extension.

definitions.note: a location phrase rather than a noun: the answer is a city found there

parts.note: N is one of the four compass points

indicators.note: the letters of has are set down wrongly, in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
VI is six in Roman numerals

indicators.note: in a down clue a rising word reads from the bottom up

parts.note: an ell is an extension to a building, a wing at right angles

explanation.surface: A tangled description of a building's extension somewhere in the state.
explanation.walkthrough: An ELL is an American term for a wing added to a house at right angles.
explanation.definitionFit: Nashville is the capital city of the state, home of country music.

clue.text: Not a real mixed up little kid, with a very high voice.

parts.note: something false is not real

indicators.note: the letters of the small child word are jumbled, as something mixed up is out of order

parts.note: a tot is a small child

explanation.surface: A confused child who is not what they seem, singing in a piercing voice.
explanation.definitionFit: A falsetto is the artificially high singing register used by male voices.

clue.text: See 25
See 6
Face the way some put it, like the osculating type.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: slang for the face or mouth, the way some put it
second meaning: one who kisses, osculate being the formal word for kiss

explanation.walkthrough: 'The way some put it' flags the first sense as slang; the second is a literal kiss-er.
explanation.definitionFit: Kisser is slang for the mouth or face, and literally a person who kisses.

clue.text: A capital arrangement for a very early boat wreck, and a letter from Athens.

indicators.note: a wreck is a ruin, so the boat letters are smashed into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
Noah's ark is about as early a boat as there is
chi is a letter of the Greek alphabet

explanation.surface: An old boat is wrecked and an arrangement is made, with a letter arriving from Greece.
explanation.walkthrough: The city was Pakistan's capital from 1947 until the government moved, hence 'A capital' rather than the current one.
explanation.definitionFit: Karachi served as Pakistan's first national capital before Islamabad was built.

clue.text: Though ginned poorly, the 4 and 27 had a happy one.

definitions.text: the 4 and 27 had a happy one
definitions.note: a descriptive phrase: the ugly duckling's story closes happily, so this means its close

indicators.note: the letters of ginned are put together badly, in another order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Even badly processed cotton, the fairy tale still finishes happily.
explanation.walkthrough: 4 and 27 together are the fairy tale's title, and fairy tales famously close with a happy outcome.
explanation.definitionFit: A story's ending is its conclusion, and a happy ending is the classic fairy-tale close.

clue.text: Likely to be sort of dead around it, but made it workable somehow.

indicators.note: the reworked dead letters sit around the word for likely
a sort of dead is a version of it, so the letters of dead are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, its four letters then rearranged
apt means likely, as in apt to fail

explanation.surface: Something seemed doomed, but someone patched it up and got it working.
explanation.definitionFit: To adapt something is to modify it so it suits a new use.

clue.text: The first of a series comprises a ratio over a large number.

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece over another puts it first

parts.note: pi is the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter
a lot is a great many

explanation.surface: An opening instalment involves a ratio sitting above a big figure.
explanation.definitionFit: A pilot is the trial first episode of a television series.

clue.text: Courage that might be 17 at first, with her top possibly getting a peace sign, and a bit of trouble.

definitions.text: Courage that might be 17 at first
definitions.note: 17 across begins with FALSE, so this is false courage, a show of boldness

parts.note: a woman's top garment, perhaps her bra
the two-finger V sign signals peace
ado is fuss or bother

explanation.surface: A woman's daring is explained via her clothes, a peace gesture and some bother.
explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference is to the start of 17 across, so the definition reads 'false courage'.
explanation.definitionFit: Bravado is a showy display of boldness meant to impress, often hiding fear.

clue.text: Early gardeners with a mad upbringing, as a well as a night out, according to the poet.

indicators.note: the letters of a mad are raised and set in a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written
and means as well as; the printed stray 'a' is a slip

parts.words: a night out, according to the poet
parts.note: eve is the poetic word for evening

explanation.surface: Gardeners with a wild childhood enjoy an evening out, poetically speaking.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue prints 'as a well as'; the stray 'a' is a slip and carries nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: In Genesis the first man and woman tended the Garden of Eden.

clue.text: Introduce Miss Gardner and Mr. Chaney in Arthur's place.

parts.note: Ava Gardner was a Hollywood film star
Lon Chaney was a silent-film actor famed for his monster roles

explanation.surface: A host introduces two Hollywood stars at King Arthur's court.
explanation.definitionFit: In legend Avalon is the island where the wounded King Arthur was taken.

clue.text: See 4 down
With flowing rills on all sides? Fixed to cut down the resistance.

definitions.text: Fixed to cut down the resistance

parts.note: rills are small streams; flowing water is a stream
something lined is edged or bordered all round

explanation.surface: A landscape edged with running brooks, then an engineer's improvement to cut drag.
explanation.definitionFit: A streamlined shape is designed to reduce air or water resistance.
